findings.claim: The change removes `this.HashCollisionResistant = copyFrom.HashCollisionResistant;` from the MessagePackSecurity copy constructor. The requirement does not ask for this, and it is a security regression. Every derived instance (for example `MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData.WithMaximumObjectGraphDepth(100)`, or any `With*` call that clones) silently falls back to non-collision-resistant hashing. That re-opens the hash-collision DoS that `UntrustedData` exists to prevent (see L4).

receipt_plan.detail: Add a test to the MessagePack unit tests: `Assert.True(MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData.WithMaximumObjectGraphDepth(100).HashCollisionResistant);` (and the same through `MessagePackSerializerOptions.Standard.WithSecurity(MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData).Security` followed by any `With*` clone). Expected: passes on base, fails on head.

findings.claim: The requirement asks that ALL generated code carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. Every template instead wraps the attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework never get it. Yet System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+ with Class as a valid target. Conditional emission is only allowed where the attribute does not exist, so these consumers are left out without cause.

receipt_plan.detail: Run tests/MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Tests/Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageTargetFrameworkSymbolTests.cs. It parses the source with NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK defined and asserts that the generated formatters and resolver carry the attribute. It fails on head.

findings.claim: The new README text says the attribute is 'only emitted for targets where it is available (not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework)'. That is factually wrong: the attribute is available on both. The docs justify the coverage gap instead of reflecting the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Compare the README statement with the netstandard2.0 reference assembly (netstandard.dll exposes System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute) and with the .NET Framework 4.0+ System.dll.

findings.claim: Ledger L9 (area codegen-templates) records the decision 'Add an opt-out setting'. The change emits the attribute with no way to opt out: there is no generator option, MSBuild property or resolver-attribute property, and every template writes the attribute unconditionally apart from the TFM #if. The recorded decision is not implemented.

receipt_plan.detail: Cite L9: 'A: Add an opt-out setting'. The hunks contain no option plumbing, and no template has a guard such as `<# if (Options...) #>` around the attribute.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Always on, no setting. Every formatter template (int-key, string-key, enum, union) and both resolver templates (including the FormatterCache and GetFormatterHelper nested classes) emit `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` with no configuration knob. The change additionally wraps it in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: On by default with an opt-out setting, as ledger L9 records ('Add an opt-out setting'). Add a boolean option that defaults to true (for example `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` in GeneratorOptions, read from an MSBuild/analyzer-config property or a GeneratedMessagePackResolver attribute property). Thread it into the template contexts and wrap each attribute emission in `<# if (Options.Generator.EmitExcludeFromCodeCoverage) { #> ... <# } #>` in the six .tt files and their regenerated .cs files. Add snapshot tests for both values and document the switch in the README.
